newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: NATO presents plans for major arms cuts.
newsitem.headline: NATO presents plans for major arms cuts.

text.p: NATO allies presented proposals for major arms cuts to a security summit on Thursday in a bid to appease Russian fears over the alliance's plans to expand eastwards.
"The alliance is prepared to take significant steps in this regard," said the proposal delivered to the body dealing with the treaty on Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE).
"Specifically, the total of future aggregate national ceilings of ground treaty limited equipment of (NATO's) 16 members will be significantly less under the adapted treaty."

A Western diplomat said the proposal, to be discussed by a working group on Tuesday, was a symbol of NATO's political goodwill towards a Russian government wary of the alliance's plans to take in former Warsaw Pact states.

"That is the key political signal of this proposal that the alliance is prepared to lower its overall force levels. We see this as unilateral steps. We say significantly so we are not talking about one or two percent here," the diplomat said.

The original CFE treaty was negotiated in 1990 under the auspices of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe to try to strike a balance between the military hardware held by NATO and the now-defunct Soviet-led Warsaw Pact.
British delegate Crispin Hain-Cole, who will chair the negotiations, said the adapted treaty, which must be signed by all 30 CFE members, would form the cornerstone of security in Europe.
"There is a genuine prize to be had from this negotiation in terms of enhanced security for all members. This is definitely not a zero sum game," he told reporters.

NATO, created during the Cold War era to defend the West from attack by the Soviet Union, has raised Moscow's shackles by planning to admit former Soviet satellites, probably starting with Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, now visiting Moscow, was expected to offer sweeteners aimed at soothing Russia, but the Kremlin made it clear it would not be won over easily.

The new NATO position, as presented to the CFE talks, clearly accepted the principle of limiting the arsenals of individual countries as opposed to regions, effectively preventing NATO from massing troops on Russia's borders.

"It will go from a system of groups -- NATO and the Warsaw Pact -- to one of each country having its own national limits for its own nationally-owned equipment and a territorial limit for its geographical territory within which many stationed forces would have to be fitted as well," Hain-Cole said.
The United States says the proposed changes to the CFE treaty would meet Moscow's demands for a legally-binding contract providing security guarantees.

Russia was the only party to the CFE treaty to fail to meet a 1995 deadline for destroying some of its military equipment. The CFE states agreed last June to extend the deadline, giving Russia until May 31, 1999 to meet its arms cuts quotas.
Hain-Cole predicted that the negotiations on the treaty revision would progress fast.

"I would fully expect there will be a consensus wish by the NATO side and by others to make substantial progress early in this period so that even by the time of the NATO Madrid summit in this negotiation here we can see the main elements of how the treaty will be adapted," he said.
NATO leaders, meeting in Madrid in July, plan to issue formal invitations to some ex-Warsaw Pact states to join the alliance.
